content: The management of individuals infected with the hepatitis C virus (HCV) is comprehensively detailed in several key documents. These include the WHO Guidelines for the Care and Treatment of Persons Diagnosed with Chronic Hepatitis C Virus Infection (2018), the WHO Guidelines on Hepatitis B and C Testing (2017), and the Recommendations and Guidance on Hepatitis C Virus Self-Testing (2021). Additional resources include the Guidelines for the Prevention, Care, and Treatment of Persons with Chronic Hepatitis B Virus Infection (2015), the Consolidated Guidelines on HIV, Viral Hepatitis, and STI Prevention, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Care for Key Populations (2022 update), and the Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Prevention, Testing, Treatment, Service Delivery, and Monitoring: Recommendations for a Public Health Approach (2021). These guidelines are primarily intended for national hepatitis program managers and policymakers in ministries of health, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). They are responsible for developing national hepatitis testing and treatment plans, policies, and guidelines. The guidelines are also valuable for laboratory managers in ministries of health, reference laboratories, and key hospital laboratories, who oversee assay validation, national testing algorithms, assay procurement, quality control (QC), and quality assurance (QA). Furthermore, healthcare providers offering hepatitis testing, care, and treatment, including those in community-based programs, will find these guidelines useful. The development and implementation of these guidelines are guided by several principles: 1. Public Health Approach: The guidelines support a public health approach to scaling up antiviral treatment for HCV infection across the continuum of hepatitis prevention, diagnosis, linkage to care, and treatment. This approach emphasizes streamlined, standardized strategies such as task sharing, decentralization, integration of HCV services with other public health programs, and patient and community empowerment. While high-income countries with more resources may adopt individualized care approaches, the overarching framework remains rooted in public health principles. 2. People-Centered Care: This approach prioritizes the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities, treating them as active participants in health systems that respond to their needs and preferences in a humane and holistic manner. It also considers the experiences of healthcare providers, which can influence the delivery of high-quality, people-centered care. 3. Enabling Environment for Key Populations: Implementing the guidelines requires efforts to promote and protect the human rights of individuals needing hepatitis services. This includes ensuring informed consent, preventing stigma and discrimination, and promoting gender equity. Structural barriers such as stigma, marginalization, criminalization, and violence disproportionately affect women, young girls, adolescents, and key populations across the HIV and hepatitis care continuum. Addressing these barriers is critical to achieving equitable access to care. The updated WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV, Viral Hepatitis, and STI Prevention, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Care for Key Populations (2022) outline essential strategies for creating an enabling environment. These include supportive legislation and policies, decriminalization of drug use and possession, addressing stigma and discrimination, empowering communities, and addressing violence against key populations. Workforce training to combat stigma and discrimination and strategies to support those affected by violence are also emphasized to ensure safer and more accessible healthcare services. HCV infection remains a significant public health challenge, causing approximately 399,000 deaths annually, primarily from cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In 2019, an estimated 58 million people were chronically infected, with a disproportionately high burden in LMICs. Transmission occurs mainly through injecting drug use, sexual transmission (especially among men who have sex with men), and unsafe healthcare practices. HCV infection is caused by six major genotypes, with geographic variations in their distribution. In May 2016, the World Health Assembly endorsed the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) on viral hepatitis, aiming to eliminate it as a public health threat by 2030. Elimination is defined as a 90% reduction in new chronic infections and a 65% reduction in mortality compared to 2015 levels. Achieving these targets requires scaling up prevention, testing, and treatment interventions to diagnose 90% of those infected and treat 80% of those diagnosed. Despite progress in some countries, significant gaps remain in the testing and treatment cascade, with only 21% of infected individuals diagnosed and 13% treated as of 2019. HCV infection can cause both acute and chronic hepatitis. Approximately 20% of individuals experience early symptoms during acute infection, and 25% achieve spontaneous clearance without treatment within six months. However, 55–85% develop chronic infection, which can lead to progressive fibrosis and cirrhosis. The risk of cirrhosis ranges from 15% to 30% after 20 years of infection. Decompensated cirrhosis and HCC may develop, with an annual progression rate of 1–3% for cirrhosis to HCC. Risk factors for progression include age at acquisition, alcohol use, HBV or HIV coinfection, and immunosuppression. HCV infection is also associated with extrahepatic manifestations, including depression, diabetes mellitus, and chronic renal disease. Immune-related conditions such as mixed cryoglobulinemia and B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma are less common but directly attributable to HCV infection. These manifestations often improve with treatment. Healthcare-associated transmission of HCV occurs in settings with inadequate infection prevention and control measures, such as unsafe injections, renal dialysis, surgery, and unscreened blood transfusions. Globally, unsafe healthcare injections account for an estimated 315,000 new HCV infections annually. Addressing this requires safer healthcare practices, reuse-prevention injection devices, and reducing unnecessary injections. Injection drug use accounts for 23% of new HCV infections globally, with 8% of current infections among people who inject drugs. These individuals face increased mortality risks due to combined factors such as low socioeconomic status, poor healthcare access, and environmental challenges. Sexual transmission of HCV is infrequent in heterosexual couples but more common among men who have sex with men, particularly those who are HIV-negative. Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) have revolutionized HCV treatment, offering high efficacy across all six major genotypes. Pangenotypic DAAs, such as sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, simplify care pathways by eliminating the need for genotyping, streamlining procurement, and expanding global treatment access. These regimens are effective in various populations, including those with HIV coinfection, compensated or decompensated cirrhosis, and renal insufficiency. However, access to DAAs remains limited in many regions due to high costs, though opportunities for low-cost generic medicines are increasing, particularly in LMICs. The updated WHO guidelines include new recommendations on DAA use in adolescents and children aged ≥3 years, simplified service delivery models, and the use of point-of-care HCV RNA viral load assays for diagnosis and cure testing. Updates also address dried blood spot testing and new data on HCV RNA viral load assay detection limits. These updates align with the modular approach adopted since 2020 to respond to emerging evidence on hepatitis B and C infections.
